title: Reproducing the FRMF Risk Analysis Template on an Open Model
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses third-party usability of an AI risk-management framework, reasonably scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Reproducing the FRMF Risk Analysis Template on an Open Model

**Problem:** The 'Frontier AI Risk Management Framework in Practice' technical report demonstrates a structured risk analysis on a frontier model, but the worked methodology has not been shown to be runnable by external parties on an accessible open-weight model, leaving its third-party usability untested.

**Direction:** Take the public FRMF risk-analysis structure (capability assessment, risk modeling, mitigation mapping) and execute a scoped version end-to-end on one open-weight model for a single risk domain (e.g., cyber-uplift), documenting every place where the template assumes internal access you don't have and how you substituted public evidence.

**Why it matters:** Whether risk-management frameworks can be exercised by outsiders determines if they enable real third-party assurance or only lab self-attestation. Single open model, public methodology, no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Frontier AI Risk Management Framework in Practice: A Risk Analysis Technical Report' (arXiv:2602.14457, Feb 2026), testing external reproducibility of its risk-analysis workflow.

title: An Open Replication Slice of Frontier AI Third-Party Auditing Criteria
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses external auditability of frontier AI safety practices.

original_idea.body:
# An Open Replication Slice of Frontier AI Third-Party Auditing Criteria

**Problem:** 'Frontier AI Auditing: Toward Rigorous Third-Party Assessment' lays out criteria for auditing safety/security practices at leading companies but, as a framework paper, doesn't demonstrate how much of an audit an unaffiliated researcher can actually complete from public evidence alone.

**Direction:** Select one company, take a defined subset of the paper's audit criteria, and conduct a public-evidence-only mock audit, scoring each criterion as fully/partially/not assessable from outside. Output a reusable 'external-auditability' annotation of the criteria set, flagging which require privileged access.

**Why it matters:** Identifies exactly which parts of third-party auditing can be done counterfactually outside labs vs. which need mandated access — a concrete input to access-policy design. Pure desk research with LLM assistance.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Frontier AI Auditing: Toward Rigorous Third-Party Assessment of Safety and Security Practices at Leading AI Companies' (arXiv:2601.11699, Jan 2026).

title: Which Dangerous-Capability Evaluations Actually Require External Model Access?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses access policy for dangerous-capability evals, a key safety governance lever.

original_idea.body:
# Which Dangerous-Capability Evaluations Actually Require External Model Access?

**Problem:** 'Expanding External Access to Frontier AI Models for Dangerous Capability Evaluations' argues for structured external access but does not granularly map which specific dangerous-capability eval methods need weights/logits/fine-tuning vs. which work via API or fully public artifacts.

**Direction:** Compile a taxonomy of published dangerous-capability eval methods, code each by the minimum access tier required (public outputs, API, logits, weights, fine-tuning), and validate the coding by attempting the lowest-tier methods on an open model. Produce an access-requirement matrix to inform graduated-access policy.

**Why it matters:** Access policy is a key governance lever; knowing the minimal access each eval needs lets regulators grant the least access sufficient — useful precisely because it's done from outside a lab. Open model, light compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Expanding External Access To Frontier AI Models For Dangerous Capability Evaluations' (arXiv:2601.11916, Jan 2026) by producing the granular access-requirement taxonomy it lacks.

title: Robustness of Open-Weight Bio Safeguards to Adversarial Fine-Tuning: A Governance-Costing Replication
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets safeguard-durability cost for open-weight marginal-risk governance via a benign proxy.

original_idea.body:
# Robustness of Open-Weight Bio Safeguards to Adversarial Fine-Tuning: A Governance-Costing Replication

**Problem:** A recent paper shows open-weight genome language model safeguards can be stripped via adversarial fine-tuning, but governance discussions lack a clear sense of the COST (compute, data, expertise) needed to defeat such safeguards — which determines the real marginal risk.

**Direction:** Without touching dangerous biological content, replicate the structure of the finding on a benign proxy: take an open model with a refusal-style safeguard on an innocuous restricted topic, measure how little fine-tuning (steps, examples, GPU-hours) removes the safeguard, and translate this into a 'safeguard-durability cost curve' for governance.

**Why it matters:** Marginal-risk governance of open weights hinges on how cheaply safeguards fall; a public cost curve is exactly the diffuse, long-horizon evidence labs won't prioritize. Single GPU, small fine-tune, benign proxy domain.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Open-weight genome language model safeguards: Assessing robustness via adversarial fine-tuning' (arXiv:2511.19299, Nov 2025), abstracting it to a benign safeguard-durability cost measurement.

title: A Reusable Coding Scheme for the Safety-Case 'Four Argument Types' Across Public Frontier Documents
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses whether assurance leans on fragile safety-case argument types.

original_idea.body:
# A Reusable Coding Scheme for the Safety-Case 'Four Argument Types' Across Public Frontier Documents

**Problem:** Recent safety-case work groups arguments into inability, control, trustworthiness, and deference, and proposes reusable templates, but no study measures which argument types frontier developers actually rely on in their published safety/assurance documents.

**Direction:** Develop a coding rubric for the four argument categories, annotate a corpus of public frontier safety frameworks and model cards, and report the distribution: how much real-world assurance rests on (the weakest) 'inability' and 'trustworthiness' arguments vs. control. Release the annotated corpus.

**Why it matters:** Reveals whether current assurance leans on argument types known to be fragile, informing what safety cases regulators should demand. Document analysis, fully public, no compute beyond LLM-assisted coding.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'A Structured Approach to Safety Case Construction for AI Systems' (arXiv:2601.22773, 2026) and the inability/control/trustworthiness/deference taxonomy, by empirically coding which argument types appear in public documents.

title: Empirically Measuring the Accountability Gap for Autonomous Agents the EU AI Act Excludes

original_idea.body:
# Empirically Measuring the Accountability Gap for Autonomous Agents the EU AI Act Excludes

**Problem:** 'Governing What the EU AI Act Excludes' argues autonomous AI agents in critical infrastructure fall through accountability gaps, but the argument is doctrinal; there is no empirical catalogue of real deployed agent behaviors that current rules fail to assign responsibility for.

**Direction:** Assemble a small structured catalogue of documented autonomous-agent deployments/incidents from public sources, and for each apply a decision tree (derived from the paper) to determine whether any party is clearly accountable under existing rules. Quantify the share of 'orphaned' cases and identify the recurring gap patterns.

**Why it matters:** Agentic AI governance is a fast-moving, under-regulated frontier; concrete evidence of accountability orphans pressures the gap closed. Public-source desk research, no proprietary access.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Governing What the EU AI Act Excludes: Accountability for Autonomous AI Agents in Smart City Critical Infrastructure' (arXiv:2605.01091, May 2026).

title: Stress-Testing Agent-Identity Standards Against Real Multi-Agent Interaction Traces

# Stress-Testing Agent-Identity Standards Against Real Multi-Agent Interaction Traces

**Problem:** The 'AI Identity: Standards, Gaps' paper catalogues gaps in agent identity/authorization standards (static scopes vs. dynamic context-dependent permissions) but does not test the gaps against actual multi-agent interaction logs.

**Direction:** Run a small open-source multi-agent framework on benign tasks to generate interaction traces, then attempt to apply the paper's identity/attribution requirements to the logs: can you reconstruct which agent did what and who is accountable? Report concrete failures where current identity primitives are insufficient.

**Why it matters:** Attribution and accountability for inter-agent actions is foundational governance infrastructure for the agentic era; demonstrating concrete failure modes is valuable prototype work doable outside any lab. Local agents, light compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'AI Identity: Standards, Gaps, and...' (arXiv:2604.23280, April 2026), testing its identified identity/authorization gaps against generated multi-agent traces.

title: How Much of the AI Provenance/Watermarking Disclosure Regime Survives Simple Transformations?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses enforceability of AI-content disclosure governance with a scoped survival study.

original_idea.body:
# How Much of the AI Provenance/Watermarking Disclosure Regime Survives Simple Transformations?

**Problem:** Recent provenance work notes C2PA signatures break on any image transformation and watermarks can be stripped, and the EU mandates visible disclosure of AI content from August 2026 — but there's little reproducible, quantified evidence of how fast disclosure-bearing signals degrade under ordinary, non-adversarial handling.

**Direction:** Take publicly available AI-generated images with C2PA credentials and/or an open watermarking scheme, apply a standardized pipeline of benign transformations (resize, screenshot, re-compress, crop, social-media upload), and measure at each step whether provenance/watermark survives. Map the survival curve to the EU disclosure requirement timeline.

**Why it matters:** If the technical backbone of mandated disclosure fails under everyday use, the regulation is unenforceable; a clean survival-curve study is exactly the diffuse, public-good evidence regulators need. Open tools, CPU/light-GPU.

**Relevant context:** Extends recent provenance/watermarking findings, esp. 'Missing the Mark: Adoption of Watermarking for Generative AI Systems in Practice and Implications under the new EU AI Act' (arXiv:2503.18156, 2025) and C2PA fragility analyses, with EU visible-disclosure obligations effective Aug 2026.

title: Translating the AI Safety Index into a Self-Service Re-Scoring Tool
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses transparent AI-safety accountability infrastructure, reasonably scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Translating the AI Safety Index into a Self-Service Re-Scoring Tool

**Problem:** The FLI AI Safety Index grades major labs on safety dimensions via expert panels, and recent framework-scoring papers echo the approach, but the methodology is not packaged so that an outsider can transparently re-derive a lab's score from public evidence as facts change.

**Direction:** Reverse-engineer the public Index rubric into an explicit, weighted scoring sheet, gather the underlying public evidence for 2-3 labs on a subset of dimensions, and compute scores reproducibly. Run a sensitivity analysis showing which dimensions/weights most change the ranking, and release the tool.

**Why it matters:** Transparent, re-runnable safety scorecards are durable accountability infrastructure independent of any single org's panel — directly extending the suggested follow-up to apply the Index methodology to additional dimensions. Public data, no compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends the AI Safety Index (FLI) methodology — flagged in the subfield context as a benchmark to apply to additional dimensions — informed by recent framework-scoring papers (arXiv:2512.01166).

title: Comparing Security-Framing vs. Innovation-Framing in National AISI Outputs: A Corpus Study
quick_reasoning: Addresses AI safety institution strategy but the link to safety outcomes is broad/indirect.

original_idea.body:
# Comparing Security-Framing vs. Innovation-Framing in National AISI Outputs: A Corpus Study

**Problem:** The subfield context flags a surprising divergence — UK AISI rebranded to 'AI Security Institute' (security framing) while US AISI became CAISI (innovation framing) — and asks whether framing affects safety outcomes, but this hasn't been studied empirically through what each institute actually publishes.

**Direction:** Assemble a corpus of public outputs from both institutes (and 1-2 others), and use a simple, pre-registered text-analysis pipeline (keyword/frame frequency, topic modeling, LLM-assisted frame labeling) to quantify how much each emphasizes security/risk vs. innovation/capability framing over time. Test whether the rebrands coincide with measurable shifts.

**Why it matters:** Empirically grounds a high-level strategic question about divergent national approaches to AI safety institutions — pure public-document analysis with strong counterfactual value. No lab access, light compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends the subfield's 'Recent Surprising Results' on UK AISI vs. US CAISI framing divergence, operationalizing the suggested follow-up via corpus analysis of institute publications.

title: Are Other Technical AI-Safety Orgs Following MIRI's Governance Pivot? A Publication-Trajectory Analysis

# Are Other Technical AI-Safety Orgs Following MIRI's Governance Pivot? A Publication-Trajectory Analysis

**Problem:** The subfield context highlights MIRI's pivot from alignment to governance as a surprising signal and asks whether other technical orgs are making similar moves, but this is asserted, not measured.

**Direction:** Build a dataset of publication/output metadata from a set of technical AI-safety orgs over recent years, classify each output as technical-alignment vs. governance/policy using a simple LLM classifier, and plot the trajectory per org. Test whether there is a detectable field-wide drift toward governance.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies a strategic field-level trend that informs where safety effort and funding should go — a meta-governance study doable entirely from public bibliographic data. No lab resources, minimal compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends the subfield's 'Recent Surprising Results' on MIRI's 2025 governance pivot (intelligence.org governance agenda / arXiv:2505.04592), operationalizing the suggested follow-up across multiple orgs.

title: Cross-Walking Seven Governance Instruments: A Machine-Readable Required-Evidence Ontology
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses harmonization of safety-evidence obligations across governance instruments.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Walking Seven Governance Instruments: A Machine-Readable Required-Evidence Ontology

**Problem:** The behavioural-assurance paper anchors its argument in 7 governance instruments with 'similar grammar' (risk management, traceable testing, incident reporting, conformity assessment) but does not produce a structured, machine-readable cross-walk of which exact evidence obligations overlap or diverge across them.

**Direction:** Extract the discrete evidence obligations from each of the 7 instruments into a normalized schema, build a cross-walk matrix of overlaps/conflicts, and compute simple metrics (shared core obligations, instrument-unique obligations). Use an LLM to draft candidate mappings and hand-verify a sample for reliability.

**Why it matters:** A machine-readable obligation cross-walk is reusable infrastructure for international harmonization of evaluation methodologies — a named open problem — and is pure public-document work. No compute beyond an LLM.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Position: Behavioural Assurance Cannot Verify the Safety Claims Governance Now Demands' (arXiv:2605.15164, May 2026), turning its 7-instrument 'shared grammar' observation into a structured cross-walk.

title: Operationalizing the Standardized AI Threat Taxonomy: An Inter-Coder Reliability Pilot
quick_reasoning: Relevant to AI security/governance standards but the safety-outcome link is fairly broad.

original_idea.body:
# Operationalizing the Standardized AI Threat Taxonomy: An Inter-Coder Reliability Pilot

**Problem:** A recent 'Standardized Threat Taxonomy for AI Security, Governance, and Regulatory Compliance' proposes a unified taxonomy, but a taxonomy is only useful for governance if different people classify the same threat the same way — and its inter-coder reliability is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Have the taxonomy applied (by you plus an LLM coder, or two prompting variants) to a sample of public AI incidents/threat descriptions, then compute agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa) per category. Identify which taxonomy categories are reliably applied vs. ambiguous, and propose definitional fixes.

**Why it matters:** Standards development needs taxonomies that produce consistent classifications across institutions; an empirical reliability check is foundational, counterfactual governance research. Public data, statistics, light compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Standardized Threat Taxonomy for AI Security, Governance, and Regulatory Compliance' (arXiv:2511.21901, Nov 2025) with an inter-coder reliability evaluation it lacks.

title: Auditing Incident-Reporting System Designs Against Real General-Purpose-AI Harms
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI incident-response governance design with a scoped validation against real harms.

original_idea.body:
# Auditing Incident-Reporting System Designs Against Real General-Purpose-AI Harms

**Problem:** 'Designing Incident Reporting Systems for Harms from General-Purpose AI' proposes a seven-dimension institutional design framework, but does not test whether documented real GPAI harms would actually be captured by a system built to those specs.

**Direction:** Take the seven design dimensions, sample real GPAI-related incidents from the public database, and trace each through a hypothetical reporting system: would it be reportable, by whom, with what required fields? Tabulate the fraction of real harms that fall outside the system's triggers and which dimensions cause the misses.

**Why it matters:** An effective national AI incident-response framework (NTSB-for-AI) is a named open problem; testing reporting-system designs against real harms before they're enacted is high-value, lab-independent work. Public data, no compute beyond LLM assistance.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Designing Incident Reporting Systems for Harms from General-Purpose AI' (arXiv:2511.05914, Nov 2025), validating its seven-dimension framework against real public incidents.

title: Mapping Emergency-Response Triggers for Catastrophic AI Risk Against Available Public Signals
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses observability of catastrophic-risk emergency triggers, a long-horizon safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Mapping Emergency-Response Triggers for Catastrophic AI Risk Against Available Public Signals

**Problem:** 'Emergency Response Measures for Catastrophic AI Risk' proposes measures and implicit triggers for activating emergency responses, but it's unclear whether the proposed triggers correspond to anything an external monitor could actually observe before it's too late.

**Direction:** Enumerate the paper's proposed emergency-response triggers, and for each assess against public information sources (incident databases, eval disclosures, compute trends) whether and how early the trigger could be detected from outside. Produce an 'observability-of-triggers' matrix flagging triggers that are effectively invisible until after harm.

**Why it matters:** Emergency response only works if triggers are observable in time; identifying blind triggers is exactly the kind of medium/long-horizon governance gap analysis labs deprioritize. Desk research, no compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Emergency Response Measures for Catastrophic AI Risk' (arXiv:2511.05526, Nov 2025) by assessing external observability of its proposed triggers.

title: Testing International AI-Agreement Verification Mechanisms Against a Toy Adversary Model
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses treaty-verification robustness, a core long-horizon safety governance lever.

original_idea.body:
# Testing International AI-Agreement Verification Mechanisms Against a Toy Adversary Model

**Problem:** 'Mechanisms to Verify International Agreements About AI Development' surveys verification mechanisms (compute monitoring, declarations, inspections) but does not provide a simple, reproducible way to reason about which mechanisms survive specific evasion strategies.

**Direction:** Build a small tabletop/game-theoretic model (a spreadsheet or short simulation) pairing each verification mechanism with a set of concrete evasion moves a non-compliant actor could take, and score detection probability and cost under stated assumptions. Run sensitivity analysis on which mechanisms are robust across adversary assumptions.

**Why it matters:** International coordination and treaty verification are core long-horizon governance levers; a transparent, re-runnable robustness model is valuable public infrastructure built with no lab resources. Light simulation, statistics.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Mechanisms to Verify International Agreements About AI Development' (arXiv:2506.15867, 2025) with a reproducible adversary-vs-mechanism robustness analysis.

title: Probing the 'Halting Dangerous AI Activities' Requirements for External Verifiability
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets external verifiability of halting dangerous AI, central to loss-of-control avoidance.

original_idea.body:
# Probing the 'Halting Dangerous AI Activities' Requirements for External Verifiability

**Problem:** 'Technical Requirements for Halting Dangerous AI Activities' specifies what would be needed to pause or halt dangerous AI development, but does not analyze how a halt could be externally verified — i.e., how an outside party confirms an actor actually stopped.

**Direction:** Decompose the paper's halting requirements into discrete technical capabilities, and for each assess what external evidence (compute telemetry, model-release patterns, public commitments) could verify compliance vs. which require trusted internal access. Output a 'halt-verifiability' map distinguishing self-attested from independently checkable requirements.

**Why it matters:** A credible ability to halt and verify halting is central to avoiding loss-of-control scenarios; clarifying what's externally verifiable is high-value, lab-independent governance work. Pure analysis, no compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Technical Requirements for Halting Dangerous AI Activities' (arXiv:2507.09801, 2025) by adding the external-verifiability dimension it does not address.

title: Quantifying the Transparency-Disclosure Gap on Loss-of-Control-Relevant Items in Model Cards
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets disclosure gaps on loss-of-control-relevant items, a precondition for verification.

original_idea.body:
# Quantifying the Transparency-Disclosure Gap on Loss-of-Control-Relevant Items in Model Cards

**Problem:** The Foundation Model Transparency Index dropped from 58 to 40 (2024 to 2025) with persistent gaps on training data, compute, and post-deployment impact, but the Index aggregates broadly and doesn't isolate disclosure specifically on the high-stakes, loss-of-control-relevant items governance frameworks now require.

**Direction:** Define a focused checklist of loss-of-control-relevant disclosure items (eval methods for autonomy/oversight-evasion, post-deployment monitoring, capability thresholds), and hand-score a set of recent public model/system cards against it. Compare your focused score to the broad Index and report where disclosure is systematically thinnest.

**Why it matters:** Transparency is the precondition for third-party verification; pinpointing the thinnest disclosures on the most dangerous capabilities directs governance attention where it matters and needs only public documents. No compute beyond LLM-assisted coding.

**Relevant context:** Extends the Foundation Model Transparency Index findings reported in the Stanford 2026 AI Index (responsible-AI chapter), narrowing its broad disclosure scoring to loss-of-control-relevant items.
